Passage-level full-text queries 'Imbabura stress', 'Ecuadorian stress', 'Salasaca stress' returned 0 hits, so the work has no Imbabura-specific stress statement in its searchable text; its Ecuadorian sketch (3.2.8) is of Salasaca (Tungurahua), not Imbabura. new_statements.rule_in_words: Across Quechua, stress is on the penultimate syllable; the only family-wide exception is word-final stress caused by the first-person marker -y (a QII feature Ecuadorian Quechua does not have, since it uses -ni), and non-penultimate systems (initial stress, syllable-structure-dependent stress) are confined to quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo in central Peru. The statement is about the Quechua family as a whole; nothing Imbabura-specific about stress appears in the searchable text.
new_statements.exceptions: word-final stress before the first-person marker -y (QII Peru/Bolivia); word-initial and syllable-structure-dependent stress in quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo; elsewhere in the book final stress in Pacaraos Quechua and in the Chachapoyas area (elision of a final vowel) -- none of these concern Ecuadorian Quechua
new_statements.identity_note: Adelaar & Muysken's stress passage is a statement about the Quechua family as a whole (section 3.2 phonology), not about Imbabura Highland Quichua specifically; the book's Ecuadorian dialect sketch is Salasaca (Tungurahua province), and no stress snippet surfaced from it. The Imbabura-specific penult statement held by the project is Ott et al. 1971 (Otavalo variety).

new_statements.quote: In most Quechua dialects stress is assigned to the penultimate vowel of each polysyllabic word form and thus provides an easy phonology-based criterion for word delimitation. Exceptionally, in interjections and emphatic expressions, stress can be word-final, e.g. in alaláw ‘how cold!’. In Tarma and the dialect of northern Junín word-final stress can occur as a result of the elision of a final syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's fixed penult (StressTyp2 < Cole 1982:208) at family level ('most Quechua dialects'); it adds nothing Imbabura-specific. Correction to the statement held by the project: the existing_statements quote ('-y that attracts stress.. Otherwise, penultimate stress is predominant. More complex, non-penultimate stress patterns.. quantity-insensitive Ancash and quantity-insensitive Cajatambo') is the PACARAOS passage on printed p.207 (first-person marker -´y in Pacaraos Quechua, Peru), not an Ecuadorian Quechua statement; the sentence that actually covers Imbabura is the general one on p.206 quoted here. The catalog reading (penult) is unaffected.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement: in most Quechua dialects (no exception is made for Ecuador/Imbabura) word stress falls on the penultimate vowel of every polysyllabic word; word-final stress only in interjections/emphatic expressions and, in certain central-Peruvian quantity-insensitive dialects, after syllable elision or a word-final first-person length morpheme; deviant (initial/weight-dependent) patterns are named only for quantity-insensitive Ancash, Cajatambo, QIIA Ferreñafe, QIIB Amazonas/Chachapoyas and Pacaraos (phonemic penult/final). The book has NO Imbabura- or Ecuador-specific stress sentence: the Ecuadorian sketch 3.2.8 (Salasaca, pp.237-242) contains no stress/accent statement (0 hits), and the Imbabura mentions (pp.193, 199, 204, 393-4) concern Cole's grammar, aspirate reflexes (f, x), *ly > ž and the f fricative, not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: nothing said about secondary stress for Quechua in 3.2.5
new_statements.exceptions: word-final stress in interjections and emphatic expressions (alaláw 'how cold!'); Tarma/northern Junín final stress after elision of a final syllable; quantity-insensitive final stress on word-final first-person long-vowel morpheme; Pacaraos phonemic stress (penult or final, -´y first person); non-penultimate, weight/initial patterns in quantity-insensitive Ancash (Huaraz rule given after Torero 1964), quantity-insensitive Cajatambo, QIIA Ferreñafe, QIIB Amazonas, and a penult-to-initial shift in Chachapoyas and some other northern Peruvian dialects (p.198). None of these concern Ecuadorian/Imbabura Quechua.
new_statements.identity_note: The work treats Quechua as a family (section 3.2.5 phonology); Imbabura Quechua (Ecuador, Otavalo area; Cole 1982) is mentioned on pp.193, 199, 204, 393-4 for segmental features only; the Ecuadorian dialect sketched in 3.2.8 is Salasaca (Tungurahua), not Imbabura.
